clue.text: Go mad -hit single's No.1!

parts.note: to hit is to strike a blow
single means one, and the possessive keeps the 's
the number one is the top, the best

explanation.surface: An excited fan cheers a chart-topping single.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation reads like pop-chart news; the pieces are simply strung together in order.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose one's temper in a fit of fury is the idiom here, matching going mad with anger.

clue.text: Composer has part set up for graduate

parts.note: Johann Sebastian Bach, the German composer

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means the word is written upwards, so read backwards

parts.note: a part in a play is a role

explanation.surface: A composer has a part composed or arranged for a university graduate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set up' reverses ROLE to ELOR, which follows BACH.
explanation.definitionFit: A Bachelor of Arts or Science is someone holding a first university degree, a graduate.

clue.text: Counterpart peer

explanation.surface: A two-word description of an aristocrat's equal in the Lords.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peer' suggests a lord, but here it means an equal.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a counterpart and a peer are a person holding the equivalent post or rank elsewhere.

clue.text: One's admitted being in possession

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to holding stolen goods.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'own up' or 'own' is to admit, so the answer can be read as one who has admitted; 'being' is a noun, a creature that possesses.
explanation.definitionFit: One who owns things holds possession of them; and to own is also to confess, so one who owns has admitted.

clue.text: Convert queries gentleman's title

indicators.note: to convert something is to change it into a different form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone tries to turn questions into a courtesy title.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Convert' rearranges the letters of QUERIES.
explanation.definitionFit: Esq. is the courtesy title written after a man's surname on formal letters.

clue.text: Attempt to incorporate old play, perhaps

indicators.note: to incorporate is to take something into one's body, so one piece is placed inside another

parts.note: an attempt is a try
old means aged

explanation.surface: A theatre company tries to stage an old play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to incorporate' puts AGED inside TRY. 'perhaps' marks the definition as an example: the answer need not be a play.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet is one example: a drama with a sad ending is a kind of stage work.

clue.text: Bird that's stopped flying over carthorse

parts.note: a bird that has landed on a branch is one that perches
on means over, as in a lid on top of a box

explanation.surface: A bird that has landed flies off again over a big working horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stopped flying' looks as if it is an anagram signal but it describes a perching bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A Percheron is a heavy French breed of draught horse used for pulling carts and ploughs.

clue.text: Talk a lot, and miss end of horror film

indicators.note: to miss the end is to drop the final letter of the film's title

parts.note: Jaws is Spielberg's 1975 shark horror film

explanation.surface: A chatterbox talks so much they miss the end of a horror film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'miss end of' removes the last letter of JAWS.
explanation.definitionFit: To talk at length is an informal verb sense, like chattering or gabbing.

clue.text: Dates arranged to deal with previous years' shortfall

definitions.text: Dates arranged to deal with previous years' shortfall

parts.words: Dates arranged to deal with previous years' shortfall
parts.note: a system of dates set up by Julius Caesar, with leap years added to fix the drift of the old Roman year

explanation.surface: An accountant reschedules payments to cover a deficit from past years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dates arranged' looks like an anagram, and 'shortfall' sounds financial; in fact the shortfall is the old Roman year running short of the solar year.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesar's reform of 46 BC set out a dating system whose leap day made up the lag of earlier years.

clue.text: For many people, daughter coming late is not hard to handle

indicators.note: coming late means the letter arrives further on in the word than before

parts.note: something known widely is known to many people

explanation.surface: A family's daughter is late, which many people find hard to handle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming late' moves the D of WIDELY two places later. The answer is a rare word, the opposite of unwieldy.
explanation.definitionFit: Something easy to wield is easy to manage, as in the commoner opposite unwieldy.

clue.text: Do better than playing chicken

parts.note: to cap a story is to top or outdo it
a show that is playing is on

explanation.surface: Someone outdoes a rival in a game of chicken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing chicken' reads as the dare game; 'chicken' is a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A capon is a castrated cockerel fattened for the table.

clue.text: Query a routine before English dance

parts.note: QU is an abbreviation for query or question
a drill is a set routine practised repeatedly

explanation.surface: A dancer asks about a routine before an English dance.
explanation.definitionFit: The quadrille is a square dance for four couples, popular in nineteenth-century ballrooms.

clue.text: Against getting into violent exercise -no longer in the army

indicators.note: getting into means entering, so one piece sits inside the other
violent means wild and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: V stands for versus, meaning against

explanation.surface: A veteran objects to strenuous drill now they have left the forces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'violent' rearranges EXERCISE into EXSERICE, and 'getting into' places V inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A former member of the armed forces is a veteran, having left military duty.

clue.text: Reported large crowd in a store

indicators.note: reported means spoken, so the word sounds like another

parts.note: a horde is a large crowd

explanation.surface: News of a big crowd gathered in a shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a store' looks like a place; 'a store' is the definition, and 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A stockpile kept hidden away, such as a miser's cash, is a store.

clue.text: Vacillations of doubter become unduly noticeable

indicators.note: vacillations are wavering movements, so the letters swing into a new order

explanation.surface: A doubter's wavering starts to attract too much attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vacillations of' rearranges DOUBTER.
explanation.definitionFit: To thrust oneself forward without invitation is to intrude, making oneself conspicuous.

clue.text: Stuff to make comfortable furniture?

parts.note: stuff is a verb: padding a chair or sofa with filling and covering it

explanation.surface: A request for material for making cosy chairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuff' looks like a noun (material), but it is a verb: to pad furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: To fit seats with padding, springs and fabric covers makes chairs soft to sit on.

clue.text: See attempt to dismiss striker

explanation.surface: Watch the bowler try to get the batsman out.
explanation.walkthrough: A see is a bishop's diocese; in cricket a yorker is a ball pitched at the batsman's feet, and to york is to bowl one.
explanation.definitionFit: The diocese of an archbishop is a see; and in cricket the verb means bowling at the striker's toes to get him out.

clue.text: See 7
Suddenly stop attending college, given icy reception?

parts.note: to freeze is to stop dead suddenly
a student at university is said to be up

explanation.surface: A student abruptly leaves college after a frosty welcome.
explanation.walkthrough: Being 'up' is the British idiom for being in residence at a university.
explanation.definitionFit: A frosty reception chills, the way a big freeze locks up rivers; the question mark flags this figurative stretch.

clue.text: Heard method to produce liquid residue

indicators.note: heard means listened to, so the word is said rather than seen

parts.note: a way is a method

explanation.surface: A cheesemaker overhears the method for making a by-product.
explanation.definitionFit: Whey is the watery part of milk left behind once curds have formed in cheesemaking.

clue.text: Spar with part of the London police force?

indicators.note: part of something follows it, so the part comes after the force's name

parts.note: Scotland Yard is the headquarters of the London Metropolitan Police
an arm is a branch or part of an organisation

explanation.surface: A boxer spars with a branch of the London police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spar' looks like boxing practice; it is a ship's pole. Scotland Yard is the London police headquarters.
explanation.definitionFit: A yardarm is either end of the horizontal pole from which a square sail hangs, a timber on a ship's mast.

clue.text: Horseman with role in classic race?

definitions.text: Horseman with role in classic race?

parts.words: Horseman with role in classic race?
parts.note: a creature half horse and half man, from a race of beings in classical myth

explanation.surface: A jockey rides in one of the classic horse races.
explanation.walkthrough: The classics are flat races like the Derby, but here 'classic' means Greek myth and 'race' a kind of being.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth a centaur has a man's upper body on a horse's body.

clue.text: Go with clean break? Clot!

indicators.note: a break shatters things, so the letters fall into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone told to go for a clean break is called an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'break' rearranges GO and CLEAN. 'Clot' looks like an insult but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To clot is to thicken from liquid to solid, as blood does.

clue.text: Dismayed silver is getting tarnished, at first

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
someone who is getting something has it

indicators.note: at first takes only the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone is upset that their silver is beginning to tarnish.
explanation.definitionFit: Being horrified or appalled by something is the sense, a strong shock.

clue.text: See 2
Being treated poorly, given this liquid lunch?

definitions.text: Being treated poorly, given this liquid lunch?

parts.words: Being treated poorly, given this liquid lunch?
parts.note: a thin porridge was the stock meal handed to paupers and prisoners

explanation.surface: Office workers grumble about a boozy lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'liquid lunch' usually means drinks; here it is thin oatmeal, the meal of workhouse inmates in Oliver Twist.
explanation.definitionFit: Thin oatmeal boiled in water was the workhouse fare of the poor.

clue.text: Liquid -mead, it's said-served where document was signed

parts.note: runny means liquid, flowing

indicators.note: it's said means spoken, so the word sounds like another

parts.note: said aloud, these words sound like MEDE

explanation.surface: Liquor is served at the historic site of a royal signing.
explanation.walkthrough: Runnymede, a meadow by the Thames, is where King John sealed Magna Carta in 1215.
explanation.definitionFit: Magna Carta was sealed at Runnymede, the meadow on the Thames west of London.

clue.text: Butler's second to identify this poet

definitions.text: Butler's second to identify this poet

parts.words: Butler's second to identify this poet
parts.note: the Irish poet William Butler wrote under his surname, which comes second after his middle name

explanation.surface: A butler's assistant is asked to recognise a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butler' looks like a servant, and 'second' suggests a letter; it is the poet's middle name, and the name after it identifies him.
explanation.definitionFit: W.B. Yeats, the Irish Nobel laureate, was named William Butler.

clue.text: Settle dispute involving referee's decision

explanation.surface: A judge settles a quarrel with a ruling.
explanation.definitionFit: An arbiter hears both sides and decides, which settles a quarrel; this verb names that judging process.

clue.text: Get rotten, having tot with the French

parts.note: to tot up is to add
le is French for the

explanation.surface: Someone goes off after a drink with the French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tot' looks like a small drink but it is a verb, to add up.
explanation.definitionFit: An egg that goes bad turns rotten; the verb means to spoil.

clue.text: Rise in rent almost finalised

indicators.note: almost finished means the word stops one letter short of its final letter

parts.note: rent, the past of rend, means torn

explanation.surface: A rent increase is nearly agreed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rent' is not money but the past of rend, torn. A tor is a rocky hill on Dartmoor.
explanation.definitionFit: A tor is a rocky hill or peak, a rise in the land.

clue.text: Finds out about outing drivers go over it carefully

parts.note: to rumble someone is British slang for discovering their secret
an outing is a trip

explanation.surface: Someone uncovers an outing, and the drivers check the plan carefully.
explanation.walkthrough: A rumble strip is a band of ridged road surface that vibrates to warn drivers to slow down.
explanation.definitionFit: Raised ridges on a road make tyres vibrate noisily, so motorists slow when crossing them.
